attachment-sst: the strange situation test (sst) is the paradigm running through most of this corpus — several source pdfs are even filed with sst in the filename. originally developed to study attachment in human infants toward their mother, adapted for dogs. it revealed that the dog–owner relationship is analogous to child–parent attachment behaviour , leading to the claim that the dog possesses a behaviour-organising 'software' that fits specifically into the human social world kovacs-fri-automaton-series. mechanics separation from the attachment figure in an unfamiliar environment evokes moderate stress and anxiety, expressed as proximity seeking (e.g. standing by the door). reunion with the caregiver evokes contact-seeking behaviours (approach, physical contact) kovacs-fri-automaton-series. attachment is bi-directional: dogs show behavioural signs toward their owner, and owners perceive the relationship as an emotional bond. why it recurs the sst is doing three jobs across the corpus: 1. evidence that dog–human social organisation is deep enough to model (miklosi-2017-ethorobotics lists attachment first among dog-derived skills for robots). 2. a rule source. "considering dogs' major behaviour patterns shown in the sst, we could define a limited number of rules that could control the behaviour of the simulated companion" — the sst is where the fuzzy automaton's rule base comes from (kovacs-fri-automaton-series). 3. a test scenario. owner/stranger presence and absence in an unfamiliar room is the worked example throughout, and the base for the exploratory behaviour model in ichikawa-numakunai-2012-roman. concrete instantiation the fuzzy-automaton states derived from it — misstheowner , anxietylevel , explorationlevel — are driven by rules over owner presence, owner-to-dog distance, stranger-to-dog distance and place familiarity (kovacs-fri-automaton-series). [!note] these inputs are all obtainable on robot-platform presence, distance and movement history are exactly what a lidar plus the dr-spaam leg detector provide. unlike facial-expression recognition, the sst input set is directly implementable on the actual hardware — see the sensing warning on robot-platform and q13 in open-questions. gaps - no primary sst source in the corpus. topál et al. (2005), gácsi et al. (2001) are cited throughout but not held — see citation-backlog. needs-source - attachment is described qualitatively; no operational thresholds (what distance counts as proximity seeking, over what duration).
conditioning: the two experimental paradigms of animal learning, and their correspondence with the two algorithm families of reinforcement learning. all of this page is from sutton-barto-2018-rl ch. 14 unless marked otherwise; the primary sources it reviews are not in the corpus (see citation-backlog). this page exists because the dog behaviour this thesis models is largely conditioned behaviour, and rl-for-behaviour-learning needs the vocabulary. the correspondence psychology reinforcement learning --- --- classical (pavlovian) conditioning prediction — policy evaluation, learning a value function instrumental (operant) conditioning control — policy improvement the defining difference between the two paradigms is whether the reinforcing stimulus is contingent on the animal's behaviour . in classical conditioning it is not; in instrumental conditioning it is. the authors are careful that this is "a convenient first approximation" and not an identity: "there is more to classical conditioning than prediction; it also involves action, and so is a mode of control, sometimes called pavlovian control" (§14.1). both kinds of learning are likely engaged in most real situations. [!note] "control" means the opposite of what ethologists mean by it in this book control means the agent influences its environment . in psychology it usually means the animal's behaviour is controlled by the stimuli it receives (stimulus control). both directions are at play; the book's focus is the agent as controller (§14 terminology). worth watching when reading this alongside the ethology sources. classical conditioning pavlov's terms, still standard: an unconditioned stimulus (us) naturally triggers an unconditioned response (ur); a neutral stimulus that reliably precedes the us becomes a conditioned stimulus (cs) and comes to trigger a conditioned response (cr). in delay conditioning the cs extends through the interstimulus interval; in trace conditioning the cs ends before the us begins. two phenomena drove the modelling literature: - blocking — if an animal has already learnt that a tone predicts the us, adding a light to form a compound cs produces little or no learning to the light. this refuted the idea that temporal contiguity alone is sufficient for conditioning (kamin 1968, via §14.2.1). - higher-order conditioning — a previously conditioned cs can itself act as a us for a further stimulus. pavlov's dog learnt to salivate to a black square that had only ever been followed by a metronome, in ten trials. hard to demonstrate above second order, because the higher-order reinforcer extinguishes when it is no longer followed by the original us. the corresponding notion in instrumental conditioning is the conditioned (or secondary) reinforcer : a stimulus that consistently predicts primary reinforcement becomes reinforcing itself. primary reinforcement is that whose "rewarding or penalizing quality has been built into the animal by evolution" (§14.2.1). this is the mechanism by which a…
emotion-attribution: people attribute emotions to artificial agents, and this facilitates interaction research-proposal. now the best-evidenced claim in the wiki — two studies in the corpus test it directly. the evidence spontaneous, unprompted attribution. in gacsi-2016-emotion-attribution, participants were given no hint that the study was about emotion and were asked only "write down briefly what is happening on each video". they spontaneously credited the robot with emotional states in 12–57% of cases depending on the emotion (dog: 31–68%), and gave reliably higher scores to emotionally loaded than to neutral clips. accurate attribution. all robot clips identified above chance; 75% mean success against the live dog's 78%, with no significant overall difference. kismet-comparable rates without a face. see emotion-recognition-benchmarks. behavioural consequences, not just reports. in lakatos-2014-emotion-attribution, participants played more (or exclusively) with the ball the robot had expressed "happiness" toward , and explained their choice by reference to the robot's inner states. attribution changed what people did. attitudes improved. nars scores dropped after interaction, for dog owners (2.00 → 1.83) and non-owners alike (2.83 → 2.08). independent of expertise. no effect of dog ownership on emotion recognition in either study. the model does not require a dog-literate user. secondary emotions too. participants could detect from greeting behaviour that the robot had transgressed a rule — guilt attribution, not merely primary affect. the counter-evidence [!warning] attribution is not automatically beneficial gacsi-2016-emotion-attribution cites petisca, dias & paiva (2014): in some cases a robot's emotion expression leads to poorer perception by humans . the paper is not in the corpus — obtain it (citation-backlog). lakatos-2014-emotion-attribution observed the mechanism directly: participants often read the robot's "fear" as indifference or reluctance and responded with anger and embarrassment — discouraging the robot, making negative comments, hands on hips. a misread negative emotion produced a hostile user reaction rather than a sympathetic one. so the premise in step 2 of thesis should be qualified: attribution helps when the expressed emotion is correctly read . since fear is reliably misread across every robot measured, this is not a marginal caveat. q8 in open-questions. design implication gacsi-2016-emotion-attribution takes an unusual and useful stance: participant impressions "by definition cannot be false" — attributing no emotion or the wrong emotion means the robot's actions were badly set, not that the user erred. that reframes evaluation as a design signal and should shape validation-study. open - under what conditions attribution helps versus misleads — the central unresolved question above. - whether attribution depends on morphology, behavioural contingency, or both. indirect evidence favours contingency: the same design worked across four…
ethorobotics: the framing discipline of this thesis, named and defined in miklosi-2017-ethorobotics: an interdisciplinary science relying on evolutionary, ecological and ethological concepts for developing social robots. the core proposal: social robots should be regarded as separate species highly adapted to their niche , and their similarity to humans — in appearance or behaviour — is irrelevant in itself , without a function that requires it. human-like features are permitted where they are optimal for the function (the paper gives simple verbal feedback and a human hand as examples), and only then. the two commitments - interspecific-hri — the human–robot relationship is inter-specific, not intra-specific. most likely a form of symbiosis in which humans experience positive fitness consequences. - function-orientedness — behaviour, embodiment and problem-solving ability should fit the robot's specific environment and function. robot construction should start from function and environment. together these license dogs as the behavioural model species, and are motivated by the reinterpretation of the uncanny-valley. the claimed advantages from the robots' side: more efficient in their niche because unconstrained by expected human similarity; more acceptable social partners than imperfect androids given the state of the art; and no gender problem, since they fall in the category of animals where gender is secondary. from the humans' side: no competition with robots (robots compete with each other); humans keep control by controlling the nature of interaction and whether the niche stays open; and humans already have the mental skills to adjust their social behaviour to differently-embodied agents that show basic social-competence. the paper also frames robot evolution ecologically: robots "survive only if their niche exists and die out if they have not performed well to the expectation of humans". why it constrains the affective work emotion recognition and expression research overwhelmingly assumes human-like agents; importing it uncritically would violate function-orientedness (q5 in open-questions). the corpus shows the alternative works — emotion-recognition-benchmarks records dog-derived body movement matching a human-like face without needing one. status well sourced now. the remaining weakness is not in the wiki but in the field: miklosi-2017-ethorobotics closes by listing its own open questions ("what is the minimally functioning social competence in ethorobots? does it depend on embodiment and/or function?... there is a long way to go"), and the empirical literature answering them is small and produced almost entirely by one network (hungarian-ethorobotics-network).
function-orientedness: an ethorobotics principle: start from function and environment, then design the best-suited agent , independent of similarity to humans miklosi-2017-ethorobotics. the ethological root is tinbergen's focus on the function of behaviour in relation to the environment in which the species evolved. applied to robotics: the robot should have a function, and its embodiment, behaviour and cognitive abilities should fit its specific environment. two arguments for it beyond the uncanny-valley escape: - robot engineering is not constrained by evolutionary continuity — it can jump between radically different designs, so there is no reason to inherit human form. - humans may not be well designed for many tasks , so uncritical copying is wasted effort. the operational test applied on every ingest: does this method require the robot to look or act human in order to work, or only to be legible ? legibility is compatible with function-orientedness; imitation is not. the corpus makes the distinction concrete. gacsi-2016-emotion-attribution rejects adding arms to a robot purely for emotional display — "it does not seem practical to add extra non-functional features, such as arms and hands... just for displaying some emotional expressions, because this would make the robot unnecessarily expensive." — and notes that most social robots "do not need verbal abilities or a human-like face to fit their original function". lakatos-2014-emotion-attribution makes the same point: robots should be "functional with regard to their roles in the human community, and their social behaviour should mirror this function as well, taking into account the embodiment and the technological constraints". now supported empirically, not just argued emotion-recognition-benchmarks is the evidence: dog-derived body movement on a faceless peoplebot reached 75%, against kismet's 73% with a purpose-built expressive face. mogirobi's 83.3% joy against kismet's 82.4%. the functional route is not a compromise — it performs equivalently, at lower hardware cost. and lakatos-2014-embodiments-demo shows the same behavioural design working across four embodiments from a bare holonomic base to an 11-dof expressive head. consequence for this thesis robot-platform has no non-functional expressive hardware at all — its leds and mecanum drive both serve primary functions. that is maximally function-oriented, and makes the platform an unusually clean test of the principle. it also means every expressive behaviour must be built from motion quality and light , with no fallback. see q4 in open-questions. tracked as q5 for the risk in the other direction: affective computing methods imported wholesale carry anthropomorphic assumptions.
habitual-vs-goal-directed: psychology's distinction between two modes of behavioural control, and its correspondence with rl's model-free/model-based distinction. from sutton-barto-2018-rl §14.5–14.6 and §15.11. psychology reinforcement learning --- --- habitual — triggered by antecedent stimuli, performed more or less automatically model-free — decisions read out of a cached policy or action-value function goal-directed — controlled by knowledge of the value of goals and of the relationship between actions and consequences model-based — decisions made by planning with an environment model an environment model has two parts: a state-transition part and a reward part. what psychologists call a cognitive map (tolman 1948) is the same thing — and, crucially, it "can be learned by supervised learning methods without relying on reward signals", then used later when motivation appears. that is the account of latent learning : rats that explored an unrewarded maze caught up almost immediately once food was introduced. the trade-off goal-directed control adapts fast to a changed environment, because changing the model changes the policy through planning, without new experience of the affected states. model-free control cannot: "for a model-free agent to change the action its policy specifies for a state... it has to move to that state, act from it, possibly many times, and experience the consequences of its actions" (§14.6). habitual control is faster to execute and more robust once the environment is stable. "the development of goal-directed behavioral control was likely a major advance in the evolution of animal intelligence." overtraining converts goal-directed into habitual the experimental evidence is outcome devaluation . adams & dickinson (1981) trained rats to lever-press for sucrose pellets, then devalued the pellets by pairing free access to them with a nausea-inducing injection. in subsequent extinction trials the injected rats lever-pressed less from the very first trial — without ever having experienced lever-pressing followed by sickness. they had combined knowledge of the outcome with the outcome's changed value: model- based control. adams (1982) then compared rats trained to 100 rewarded presses against an overtrained group at 500. devaluation strongly suppressed pressing in the first group and had "little effect" in the overtrained group — "if anything, it made it more vigorous". extended training had converted goal-directed behaviour into a habit. daw, niv & dayan (2005) explain the shift by confidence-weighted arbitration : both processes run, each proposes an action, and the more trustworthy one wins. early on the model-based process is more trustworthy because chaining short-term predictions needs less experience; later the model-free process wins because planning accumulates model error and shortcuts like tree-pruning. the authors note that not every psychologist accepts the cognitive reading of devaluation experiments, "but the model-based planning…
interspecific-hri: human–robot interaction should be represented as an inter-specific relationship rather than an intra-specific one — an interaction between two different kinds, "characterised by not only different anatomy but also distinct communicational abilities" miklosi-2017-ethorobotics, gacsi-2016-emotion-attribution. originally proposed in miklósi & gácsi (2012), on the utilization of social animals as a model for social robotics — cited by nearly every source in the corpus and not itself held . see citation-backlog. why the analogy is apt lakatos-2014-emotion-attribution gives the clearest statement of what human–animal interaction shares with human–robot interaction, and human–human interaction does not: property human–human human–animal / human–robot --- --- --- symmetry symmetric asymmetric onset develops from birth may start at any age language based on language non-verbal on one side complexity very complex much simpler because human–human interaction is symmetric, lifelong and language-based, robot designers mimicking it will never produce a convincing "human" — and the mismatch between appearance and behaviour violates user expectations, producing unease. that is the uncanny-valley restated as a design failure. consequences - the robot is measured by whether the interaction works , not by how human it seems. aligns with function-orientedness. - cross-species social competence becomes the relevant precedent, which is what justifies dog-human-interaction-model. - evaluation should target acceptance and cooperation, not likeness — see validation-study. - partnership is an outcome of interaction, not a property of the robot (social-competence). robots are "constructed for a social process and not for a social state". what the framework still does not say it does not specify how emotion should work across the species boundary — which is precisely this thesis' territory. the framework licenses an affective layer via emotion-attribution but supplies no model; the model comes separately from panksepp-affective-systems via szabo-2011-emotional-engine. the join between the ethological framing and the affective architecture is made by analogy , not derived. worth noting as a soft spot in thesis.
ostensive-signalling: verbal and visual cues that mark communicative intent — signals that say "this is addressed to you" before the content arrives. was the thinnest page in the wiki relative to its importance, resting on two unresolved references. both are now held : topal-2014-ostensive ( [3] ) and albuquerque-2016-emotion-recognition ( [4] ). what an ostensive signal is a cue that gives evidence of the communicator's intention to convey information — separate from the information itself. from sperber & wilson's relevance theory and csibra & gergely's natural pedagogy , as presented in topal-2014-ostensive. the key claim: ostensive cues do not work by grabbing attention. if they did, "any loud noise" would serve equally well. they work because the recipient is disposed to read them as a precursor to communication addressed to oneself . two intentions are distinguished and can be recognised separately: the communicative intention (that i am being addressed) and the informative intention (what i am being told). what dogs do with them topal-2014-ostensive's own four-point summary: 1. dogs treat ostensive signals as indicating that they are being instructed , not as mere discriminative cues — and this is "often indispensable" to their responding to referential gestures such as pointing or gaze shift. 2. eye contact is the strongest ostensive signal. high-pitched dog-directed speech ("doggerel", the analogue of motherese) is secondary but important. name-calling is of minor importance — dogs respond the same to their own name and to an unfamiliar one (kaminski et al. 2012). 3. ostensively cued behaviour "can often act as imperatives ", inducing a "ready-to-obey" attitude. hand-reared wolves show no comparable responsiveness. 4. non-ostensive attention-getters also affect responses, but dogs' specific responsiveness rests on perceiving communicative intention. eye contact is ambivalent, not simply positive. between dogs it signals dominance and ritualised aggression; with an unfamiliar human in a threatening approach it evokes fear and raises heart rate. the communicative reading is an interspecific special case — an infant-like predisposition overriding a wolf-like aversion. the limit, and the reframing that matters most dogs meet two of three criteria for being a recipient in pedagogical knowledge transfer. they are sensitive to ostension and understand referential cueing, but ostensive signals do not produce the infant's expectation of generic information. in dogs the attitude is "ready-to-learn or ready-to-obey" and "largely tied to the here and now". so the authors reconceive the adaptive function: not (only) knowledge acquisition from human partners but as facilitating behavioural synchronisation in order to avoid conflicts and/or to co-act in terms of common actions without necessarily comprehending the causal structure of the collaborative interaction. no mind-reading is required — dogs "grasp the explicit or overt dimension of communication without any…
social-competence: the target property for an ethorobot. defined in miklosi-2017-ethorobotics as an individual's ability to generate social skills that conform to the expectations of others and the social rules of the group. it emerges only when three conditions hold: the individual wants to participate, has the means to participate, and is regarded by others as able to participate. that third condition is the interesting one for robotics — social competence is partly conferred by the partner, not wholly built into the agent. which is why: partnership is a process, not a state "a social robot does not automatically become a social partner but achieves this state of affairs if it engages in the appropriate kind of social interactions with its partner. any type of partnership is not an a priori attribute of the robot but actually an outcome of relevant social interactions." — miklosi-2017-ethorobotics both the robot's social skills and the time devoted to interaction by both parties determine whether partnership emerges. consequence for validation-study : a single 20-minute session cannot measure social competence in this sense; it can only measure legibility of expression. every empirical study in the corpus (lakatos-2014-emotion-attribution, gacsi-2016-emotion-attribution) is a short single-session study, so none of them actually tests the framework's central construct. that is a real gap, and a possible contribution. habitual-vs-goal-directed now offers a candidate mechanism and instrument for that gap — a documented shift from goal-directed to habitual control with repeated experience, detectable by outcome devaluation. q16 in open-questions. why the human model is rejected approaches like fong et al. (2003) enumerate the human social skills a robot should have. miklosi-2017-ethorobotics rejects this on two grounds: there is no robust technical solution for most of them, and the biological foundations of human social interaction are obscured by our social and cultural complexity. the dog's competence is simpler and legible — which is the whole argument for dog-human-interaction-model. dog-derived components proposed for robots from miklosi-2017-ethorobotics: - attachment to humans (attachment-sst) - simple ways of communicative interaction - responsiveness to learning and training — see below - being useful in some specific way [!important] "responsiveness to learning and training" is the in-corpus mandate for rl this item sat unremarked until the sutton-barto-2018-rl ingest. it is a requirement stated by the framing source of the whole thesis, and no system in the corpus satisfies it — every model is hand-authored and fixed at design time (fuzzy-automaton-fri, szabo-2011-emotional-engine). it is therefore the strongest justification available for the decision recorded in rl-for-behaviour-learning: a trainable robot is not an imported machine-learning ambition but an unmet ethorobotic requirement. it also picks the method — skinner's shaping (conditioning) is…
uncanny-valley: mori's 1970 hypothesis: affinity toward an agent rises with human likeness, then collapses in a narrow band of very-close-but-imperfect similarity, before recovering at perfect humanness miklosi-2017-ethorobotics. the dependent variable (japanese shinwakan , "affinity") has two maxima — the medium peak at roughly 60–75% similarity, and the maximum peak at (near-)perfect similarity — with the valley between them. prior explanations divide into evolutionary (threat/death avoidance), developmental (appears in infants only after ~12 months), and perceptual/mental (competing mental representations). all assume the effect is specific to humans and to artificial creatures. the ethorobotics reinterpretation miklosi-2017-ethorobotics argues the effect is a special case of a general biological requirement: agents must categorise others accurately — conspecific vs heterospecific, familiar vs unfamiliar, individual vs group member — because the category determines what actions to take and what responses to expect. on that reading, mori's x-axis is really the conspecific/heterospecific boundary: - medium peak = interaction with heterospecifics sharing many human attributes — e.g. domesticated animals. - maximum peak = interaction with conspecifics. - conspecific recognition is far more selective (mismating with hybrids or close relatives is costly), which is why the maximum peak has a narrower base . the paradox, and why it matters here passing the valley solves nothing. technology will not stop at human parity — a robot can have 360° vision where a human has gaze-following. so "trans-human" and then "post-human" robots fall into a second uncanny valley on the far side. the landscape is symmetric; humans avoid both the less and the overly human-like miklosi-2017-ethorobotics. therefore: go around the peak, not over it. occupy a different niche defined by function (function-orientedness). this is the argument that makes ethorobotics a position rather than a preference, and it is why the dog model follows (dog-human-interaction-model). status of the evidence the hungarian engineering papers treat the valley cautiously and consistently: "although many take this effect for granted, only little actual research was devoted to this issue", and for 3d robots "the answer is presently less clear" (kovacs-fri-automaton-series, vincze-2012-interfaces-and-virca). worth keeping in view: the whole ethorobotics case rests partly on a hypothesis its own proponents describe as under-evidenced. mathur & reichling (2016) and ferrey et al. (2015) are cited but not in the corpus — see citation-backlog.

actor-critic: the rl architecture that maps most cleanly onto both the mammalian brain and the structure this thesis already has. from sutton-barto-2018-rl §13.5, §15.7–15.8 and §15.10. the structure two components learning simultaneously from the same signal: - the critic learns a state-value function for whatever policy the actor is currently following, using a td method (td-learning). - the actor holds the policy and updates it from the critic's td error. "a positive δ means that the action was 'good' because it led to a state with a better-than-expected value; a negative δ means that the action was 'bad'." the critic has no direct access to the action; the actor has no direct access to the reward. the same δ reinforces both, but with opposite objectives: the actor works to keep δ as positive as possible; the critic works to drive δ toward zero (§15.8). [!important] the only structural difference between actor and critic is the eligibility trace the critic's traces are non-contingent (presynaptic activity only) — making its learning rule "essentially the td model of classical conditioning". the actor's are contingent (they also depend on the unit's own output) — making its rule "like instrumental conditioning using a law-of-effect-type learning rule". "the difference between the critic and actor learning rules is relatively simple, but this difference has a profound effect on learning and is essential to how the actor–critic algorithm works." (§15.8) this is the same prediction/control split as conditioning, realised as one line of algebra. the critic solves the delayed-reward problem for the actor: "the td error produced by the critic acts as a conditioned reinforcement signal for the actor, providing an immediate evaluation of performance even when the primary reward signal itself is considerably delayed" (§14.4). the neural hypothesis following takahashi, schoenbaum & niv (2008), §15.7 places the actor in the dorsal striatum and the critic's value-learning in the ventral striatum , with dopamine neurons in the vta and snpc broadcasting δ to the corticostriatal synapses of both. three facts of neuroanatomy make this fit: dopamine axons target both striatal subdivisions; dopamine appears critical to synaptic plasticity in both; and the effect of a neuromodulator depends on the target structure, so one broadcast signal can drive two different learning rules. dopamine neurons are unusually well suited to broadcasting a scalar: each axon makes roughly 500,000 synaptic contacts, 100–1,000 times more than a typical neuron. two cautions the authors give: - modern evidence points to "the more complicated picture that different subpopulations of dopamine neurons respond to input differently", i.e. the signal may be vector-valued rather than scalar (§15.4). - lesion work shows the actor placement is "too simple": the dorso lateral striatum is more involved in model-free/habitual processes, the dorso medial in model-based/goal-directed ones (§15.11). see…
behaviour-trees: the execution layer of emotion-engine, and — following csenge's decision of 2026-07-28 — the executive method for decisions made by reinforcement learning algorithms . py trees and py trees ros are installed on robot-platform and already in use in mecanumbot-behaviours. primary source: colledanchise-ogren-behavior-trees. how a bt works a bt is a directed rooted tree in which internal nodes are control flow nodes and leaves are execution nodes. the root emits ticks at some frequency; a node runs only if ticked , and returns one of three statuses to its parent: running , success , failure . node symbol semantics --- --- --- sequence → tick children left to right; return failure or running as soon as a child does; success only if all succeed fallback ? tick children left to right; return success or running as soon as a child does; failure only if all fail parallel ⇒ tick all children; success if m succeed, failure if n−m+1 fail decorator — custom transformation of a child's status (e.g. negation) action / condition leaf do something / test something fallback is also called selector or priority selector . why not an fsm — the argument that actually matters the tradeoff between reactivity and modularity in fsms is a one-way control transfer problem — the goto statement. to be reactive an fsm needs many transitions; many transitions are many one-way transfers, and as dijkstra put it that is "too much an invitation to make a mess of one's program". remove one component and every transition into it must be revised. bts use two-way control transfers governed by internal nodes. a leaf is written without knowing which node runs next — only what status to return. — colledanchise-ogren-behavior-trees §1.2, §2.6.1 everything else follows from this: modularity, reusable subtrees, hierarchical organisation, readability, and suitability for automatic synthesis. bts generalise fsms, hierarchical fsms, the subsumption architecture, teleo-reactive programs and decision trees (ch. 2, formalised in ch. 6). so choosing a bt does not forfeit anything those architectures could express. the rl integration this is why the source was ingested. colledanchise-ogren-behavior-trees ch. 8 describes rl-bt : start from a hand-designed bt and replace selected nodes with learning nodes — - a learning action node wrapping q-learning over a locally defined state, action set and reward; and - a learning control flow node , a fallback that learns the order to try its own children given the state. emotion-arbitration: the step between having an emotional state vector and doing something about it: which emotion, of several simultaneously active, gets expressed? the wiki did not have this concept before ingesting szabo-2011-emotional-engine; it is a required component of emotion-engine. two approaches in the corpus winner-take-all — kismet's approach. the strongest dimension is expressed. simple; produces abrupt switching and cannot express ambivalence. hierarchical rule tree — szabo-2011-emotional-engine, explicitly proposed against winner-take-all: 1. exactly one positive dimension → express it. 2. several positive dimensions: - a. fear 3 (medium) → express fear , regardless of all others; - b. a strict maximum exists → express it; - c. tie → fixed hierarchy fear surprise anger happiness = despair ; - d. tie at ≥ 3 → express the top two as mixed or alternating behaviour . a team of units under one broadcast signal — a third option, from sutton-barto-2018-rl §15.10 and actor-critic. several behaviour units each receive the same scalar reinforcement signal δ, each explores independently, and the expressed behaviour is their collective output. no explicit selection rule at all. williams (1992) showed such a team ascends the gradient of the shared reward without the units communicating. [!important] arbitration and credit assignment are the same question §15.10 recasts winner-take-all not as a naïve default but as a deliberate simplification of structural credit assignment : "an extreme case is a winner-take-all arrangement (for example, the result of lateral inhibition in the brain) that restricts collective actions to those to which only one, or a few, team members contribute. in this case the winners get the credit or blame." once behaviour is learnt (rl-for-behaviour-learning), this matters concretely. a hierarchical rule tree gives no way to attribute an outcome back to the components that produced it, because the rule, not the outcome, decides. winner-take-all does. the choice of arbitration scheme therefore constrains what can be learnt , which is an argument the corpus does not contain and which partly reopens the case for the option szabó et al. rejected. rule-based knowledge representation (rules are what ethologists produce), - state-machine structure (behaviour follows observed sequences), - continuous values and states . a fuzzy automaton satisfies all three: the state is a vector of membership values, state transitions are governed by a fuzzy rule base, observations and conclusions are continuous. formally, extending the fuzzy finite-state automaton to continuous inputs: the rule-base explosion, and fri a classical fuzzy rule base for δ is exponential : ( n = state-vector length, m = input dimension, i , j = term-set sizes). for an ethological model of 10–20 state variables that means thousands of rules — while the actual ethological knowledge amounts to a few dozen. most rules would be undefined, which classical fuzzy reasoning cannot handle. fuzzy rule interpolation (fri) removes the problem: the rule base may be sparse , and fri still produces a reasonable interpolated conclusion when no rule fires under the current observation. only the significant rules need to exist. five (the method used) adopts the vague environment concept: fuzzy partitions are handled by scaling functions, which turns fuzzy interpolation into crisp interpolation, then applies shepard-operator interpolation for cheap multidimensional evaluation. available as a matlab fri toolbox. the two properties that matter for this thesis low computational demand — the authors repeatedly claim the structure is "quick enough to fit the requirements of real-time embedded applications". never benchmarked in any paper in the corpus, but the claim is architectural, not empirical, and plausible. human-readable rules — "even after numerical optimization of the model, the rules are still human readable, and helps the formal validation of the model by the ethological experts". this is a genuine advantage over a learned controller and is the strongest argument against replacing this layer with reinforcement learning. td-learning: the central algorithmic idea of sutton-barto-2018-rl — the authors call ch. 6 "the most important for the subject and for the rest of the book" — and the point where the book makes contact with animal behaviour and with the brain. the td error for state values, the td error is the discrepancy between an earlier and a later estimate of expected future reward. learning updates parameters in proportion to δ and to an eligibility trace. two distinctions the book insists on, both relevant to this wiki: - reward signal vs reinforcement signal. the reward signal r defines the problem; the reinforcement signal is "the major factor directing changes a learning algorithm makes in an agent's policy, value estimates, or environment models" — for td methods that is δ, not r (§15.2, §14 terminology). inside δ, r {t+1} is the primary reinforcement contribution and γv(s {t+1}) − v(s t) is the conditioned reinforcement contribution — the formal counterpart of the secondary reinforcer in conditioning. - reward vs value. reward is immediate desirability, value is long-run desirability. "rewards are in a sense primary, whereas values, as predictions of rewards, are secondary... it is much harder to determine values than it is to determine rewards" (§1.3). the td model of classical conditioning the td algorithm doubles as a model of animal learning (§14.2.3). it generalises the rescorla–wagner model by moving from trial level to real time, t now indexing time steps of the order of 10 ms rather than whole trials. two things follow that rescorla–wagner cannot produce: - higher-order conditioning falls out of bootstrapping — since v(s {t+1}) − v(s t) appears in δ alongside r {t+1} , "as far as learning is concerned there is no difference between a temporal difference and the occurrence of a us" (§14.2.3). - timing effects within a trial — dependence of learning on the interstimulus interval, anticipatory conditioned responses, and the prediction that temporal primacy overrides blocking : a newly added cs whose onset precedes the pretrained cs is not blocked, and the pretrained cs loses associative strength. this was a prediction of the model before it was observed; kehoe, schreurs & graham (1987) later confirmed it in the rabbit nictitating membrane preparation, and noted that non-td models have difficulty explaining the data (§14.2.4). stimulus representation matters more than the algorithm. three representations are compared (§14.2.4): presence (one feature per cs while it is present), complete serial compound (csc — a tapped delay line, a precise internal clock), and microstimulus (overlapping internal signals that broaden and weaken with elapsed time). the authors call the csc "a useful fiction", unrealistic as a hypothesis about the brain, and say the common view that it is an essential part of the td model "is mistaken". which one is used determines whether the model reproduces the shape and timing of the conditioned response at all. belle-2019-programming-with-affect: shakir belle, curtis gittens (university of the west indies, barbados) and t.c. nicholas graham (queen's university, kingston), programming with affect: how behaviour trees and a lightweight cognitive architecture enable the development of non-player characters with emotions , ieee gem 2019 , pp. 1–8. reference [9] / [10] of research-proposal, now held — the last unheld numeric reference, and the one flagged as most important after colledanchise-ogren-behavior-trees turned out to contain no emotion content. what it is emobet (emotion modelling behaviour tree): a framework that makes mood a first-class property of a behaviour tree, by adding two node types. new node function --- --- emotion adder triggers an emotion in the character. single child. the developer supplies the possible emotions (from the occ set) and the triggers that fire them e-selector selects an action based on current mood . exactly two children, labelled positive and negative; picks the one matching the sign of the character's mood octant the stated motivation is that existing tools "do not treat mood as a first-class property: specifically, they do not provide mechanisms for modifying an npc's mood, or for allowing the npc's current mood to influence its behaviour." the architecture built on alma (gebhard's a layered model of affect ), reimplemented light-weight so it runs in real time on ordinary gaming hardware. four subsystems: - personality — the five factor model (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism). sets the character's default mood and scales emotion intensity: "having a highly neurotic personality will cause the intensities of negative emotions to be higher". - emotion — short-term states from occ (ortony, clore & collins). each carries type, intensity and trigger. - mood — mid-term, and "the deciding factor for all npc decisions". represented in pad space (pleasure, arousal, dominance, each −1…1), giving eight octants : exuberant, dependent, relaxed, docile, hostile, anxious, disdainful, bored. intensity is slight , moderate or full by distance from the origin. - memory — long- and short-term, decaying on the ebbinghaus forgetting curve . on re-encountering a player the character recalls its strongest memory of them and re-triggers the associated emotions. mood updates via an emotion centre — the combined pad point of all felt emotions. if the emotion centre lies between the current mood and the origin, mood is pushed further into its current octant; otherwise mood moves toward the emotion centre. three design requirements are stated: influence (emotion must affect decisions), persistence (emotions do not vanish after the event), and interface (use behaviour trees, because developers already know them). why this matters for the thesis [!important] the nearest prior art to the decision layer — and it stops where the rest of the corpus stops this is the only source in the corpus that joins emotion to behaviour trees , and it genuinely…
colledanchise-ogren-behavior-trees: michele colledanchise and petter ögren, behavior trees in robotics and ai: an introduction . crc press, 2018. [!note] provenance — this is the arxiv version the pdf in raw/ is arxiv:1709.00084v6, dated 25 october 2022 , printed from a browser. it is not the crc press print edition, and it is four years newer than the published book. cite by chapter and section , not page number. replaces the 45-page preview clipped earlier the same day. why it is here : csenge's decision, 2026-07-28 — behaviour trees as the executive layer for decisions made by reinforcement learning algorithms . this book is the standard reference for bts and, in chapter 8, contains the specific literature on combining them with rl. takeaways - a bt is a switching structure, not a state machine. internal nodes are control flow nodes (sequence → , fallback ? , parallel ⇒ , decorator); leaves are execution nodes (action, condition). the root emits ticks at a frequency; a node executes only if ticked, and returns running , success or failure to its parent. - the central argument is two-way control transfer. fsm transitions are one-way control transfers — dijkstra's goto . reactivity requires many transitions; many one-way transfers destroy modularity, because removing a component means revising every transition into it. bts use two-way transfers governed by internal nodes, so a leaf is written without knowing what runs next . this is the whole book in one idea. - bts generalise fsms, hierarchical fsms, the subsumption architecture, teleo-reactive programs and decision trees (ch. 2, formalised in ch. 6). - chapter 8 is the reason this source matters here — see below. - analysis tooling exists : ch. 5 gives a state-space formalism for safety, robustness and efficiency; ch. 9 converts stochastic bts into discrete time markov chains and computes mean time to succeed, mean time to fail and success probability over time, and shows these compose across subtrees. - honest about limits : §2.6.2 lists real disadvantages (below). chapter 8 — the rl integration, and what it says about this thesis two learning approaches, and the comparison between them (§8.4) is the load-bearing passage. rl-bt (§8.3) — start from a manually designed bt and replace a subset of nodes with learning nodes , of two kinds: - learning action node — encapsulates q-learning with user-defined state, action set and reward. their example: an action "pick an object" learns grasping, where state is object pose, actions are grasp poses, reward is grasp quality. - learning control flow node — a fallback with flexible child ordering . given a state, it learns the order in which to try its own children . reward can be task-dependent or simply return-value-dependent (positive for success, negative for failure). gp-bt (§8.2) — genetic programming builds and extends the bt itself , starting from a single action learn node, greedily trying single actions first and invoking gp only when no single action improves the reward.…

open-ended questionnaire first, then forced choice, to avoid priming. behaviour derivation is the methodologically important part: dog emotional behaviours were extracted from a meta-analysis of prior ethological studies in named contexts (joy = greeting the owner / going for a walk; anger = facing a threatening stranger; fear = facing a threatening stranger; sadness = separation / being scolded; neutral = 'mobile owner' task), then re-expressed within the robot's embodiment — not copied. see dog-human-interaction-model. robot vocalisations were synthesised to follow morton's rules (as dog barks do): aggressive = low-pitched, noisy, fast-pulsing; joyful = raised pitch, less noisy, fast-pulsing; sad = elongated, slow-pulsing, decreasing pitch. fear and neutral had no sound, because dogs rarely vocalise in those contexts. results - participants spontaneously attributed emotions to the robot (12–57% by emotion) and the dog (31–68%) with no prompting about emotion. - forced choice: all dog and all robot clips identified above chance (all p "from the viewpoint of robot development, participants' impressions by definition cannot be false. their subjective evaluation can best validate the robot's expressive behaviours." attribution of no emotion, or of the "wrong" emotion, means the robot's actions were badly set — not that the participant erred. directly relevant to designing validation-study. limitations - neutral lab, no social context, no interaction — the authors say results should not be extrapolated to real life, where context strongly aids attribution. this is exactly the gap the thesis claims to address (real-time, real environments — see emotion-engine). - video clips, not live interaction. robot teleoperated. - narrow sample (university students, 18–26). - neither the dog nor the robot could fully approach the viewer, which the authors believe depressed recognition rates. [!warning] tension with the thesis premise the introduction cites petisca, dias & paiva (2014) that in some cases robot emotion expression leads to poorer perception by humans . research-proposal assumes affect straightforwardly "helps cooperation and acceptance". the condition under which it helps is…

collaboration network extended to japan (hungarian-ethorobotics-network) — but it is the only application-domain work in the corpus. shared setting intelligent space (ispace) : an environment instrumented with distributed intelligent network devices (dinds = sensors + processors + network devices), able to track multiple people simultaneously in different locations. a mobile robot serves as the physical agent that delivers information wherever the caregiver happens to be. application : elderly monitoring / home-care support. the robot must inform a caregiver of events without disrupting their primary activity. this is a concrete answer to what a socially competent robot is actually for — the functional niche that function-orientedness demands but research-proposal never specifies. ichikawa et al. — behavioural factors extends the existing dog-based robot behaviour model by adding behavioural factors that give the same behaviour different characteristics (a personality/ temperament layer). subjects evaluated their impressions of the robot under different factor settings, in a simulator . result: subjects formed the impressions the authors expected from the factors chosen, without any prior knowledge about the robot . conclusion drawn: factors can be tuned to a caregiver's preference. numakunai et al. — exploratory behaviour adds an exploratory behaviour model, taking dogs' exploration in the strange situation test (attachment-sst) as the base. contribution: a map-building method that records not just the positions of people and the robot kovacs-fri-automaton-series: [!note] four papers, one contribution these four are a conference series with heavily overlapping text — the same fri fuzzy automaton, the same mogirobi worked example, largely the same literature review. they are filed as one source page because separating them would imply four distinct contributions. cite the specific venue when the distinction matters: - syroco'09 — interpolation based fuzzy automaton for human-robot interaction. first statement. - sami 2010 — fuzzy automaton based human-robot interaction. - hsi 2011 — ethologically inspired robot behavior implementation. adds the behaviour-based control decomposition. - coginfocom 2011 — a novel, ethologically inspired hri model implementation: simulating dog-human attachment. frames the work around the strange situation test. the problem they solve ethological models are descriptive verbal models : a sparse collection of observed action–reaction rules, not a complete specification. two consequences: 1. a state machine is the natural structure, since the models follow observed event sequences; and states are continuous, so a fuzzy automaton. 2. but a classical fuzzy rule base is exponential in the state-vector length and input dimension — r = n·iⁿ·jᵐ . for 10–20 state variables that is thousands of rules, while the actual ethological knowledge is a few dozen. fuzzy rule interpolation (fri) resolves the contradiction: the rule base may be sparse , and fri still yields a reasonable interpolated conclusion when no rule fires. their five method uses the vague environment concept and scaling functions to turn fuzzy interpolation into crisp interpolation, then applies shepard-operator interpolation for cheap multidimensional evaluation. see fuzzy-automaton-fri. two properties they emphasise, both directly relevant to this thesis: - low computational demand — "quick enough to fit the requirements of real-time embedded applications". a real-time claim, though never benchmarked. - human-readable rules — even after numerical optimisation, "the rules are still human readable, and helps the formal validation of the model by the ethological experts". a genuine advantage over a learned model. the worked example mogirobi in an unfamiliar room with owner and stranger, modelling the strange situation test (attachment-sst). fuzzy states: misstheowner , anxietylevel , explorationlevel . sample rules: run: owner leaves at step 17, stranger enters at 31 → anxiety and missing-the-owner rise, room exploration is abandoned. the output function ω: s×x→y decomposes into parallel component behaviours plus behaviour fusion, giving the standard behaviour-based control structure. relationship to the emotional engine [!warning] two separate architectures in the same research programme this series and the szabó engine are parallel, not integrated . kovács et al. model behaviour state (anxiety, exploration, missing-the-owner) with a fuzzy automaton; szabó et al. model emotional state (happiness, fear, anger, despair…

lakatos-2014-emotion-attribution: the companion empirical study to gacsi-2016-emotion-attribution, and the more directly relevant of the two: live interaction rather than video, and it tests a secondary emotion (guilt), not just primary ones. design robot : mogirobi (bme mechatronics + elte ethology) — mobile, with a 3-dof head, 2-dof neck, 1-dof ear-like appendices and a 2-dof rear antenna. the antenna and appendices deliberately bear little physical resemblance to a dog's tail and ears; they are functional analogues , not imitations. see prior-robot-platforms. both experiments were wizard-of-oz — teleoperated from an adjoining room, participants unaware. family dog project lab, elte. four cameras, solomon coder for behavioural coding, non-parametric statistics throughout. ethics approval from the elte institute of biology irb. experiment 1 (n = 48 analysed of 71) — play with two balls. the robot showed canine 'happy' behaviour (raised antenna/appendices, antenna wagging, approaching, retrieving) toward a 'preferred' ball and canine 'fearful' behaviour (lowered antenna and appendices, backing, maximising distance) toward a 'non-preferred' ball, counterbalanced by colour and order. experiment 2 — guilt attribution: could participants tell from the robot's greeting behaviour whether it had transgressed a rule? results - happiness recognised 83.3% in forced choice; fear only 47.9% — about as many participants read the robot as indifferent or emotionless as read it as fearful. - compare kismet (human-like face): joy 82.4%, fear 47.1%. probo: joy 100%, fear 65%. the dog-derived body-movement approach matched a humanoid face without needing one. see emotion-recognition-benchmarks. - participants played more (or exclusively) with the 'preferred' ball , and explained their choice by reference to the robot's inner states. - experiment 2: participants could detect transgression from greeting behaviour — a secondary emotion read successfully. - nars (negative attitudes towards robots scale) dropped after interaction (dog owners 2.00 → 1.83; non-owners 2.83 → 2.08). brief interaction improved attitudes. limitations the authors state - the ball preference may be explained by the robot's inactivity toward the non-preferred ball rather than by attributed emotion. the confound is acknowledged, not resolved. - participants often read 'fear' as indifference or reluctance , and responded with anger or embarrassment — discouraging the robot, negative comments, hands on hips. a mis-read negative emotion produced a negative user reaction. - wizard-of-oz: nothing here tests an autonomous system. the engine this thesis builds is precisely what was faked in these studies — see emotion-engine. - fear recognition being poor is consistent with dog owners also being bad at recognising fear in real dogs from visual signals alone (wan et al.). why this matters for the thesis it supplies the evaluation template for validation-study: wizard-of-oz baseline, pre/post nars, open-ended before forced-choice…

miklosi-2017-ethorobotics: this is almost certainly reference [1] of research-proposal — it is the paper that names and defines ethorobotics, and it is co-authored by korondi, who supervises the hungarian robotics side of this literature. treat the identification as strong but not confirmed until csenge verifies. the theoretical foundation of the thesis. peer-reviewed, widely cited. argument 1. social robotics is misguided in chasing human likeness. mori's uncanny valley is the only serious hypothesis about human–robot affinity, and it predicts the opposite of the field's intuition (uncanny-valley). 2. reinterpreted ethologically, the valley is not robot-specific. it reflects a general biological need to categorise other agents — conspecific vs heterospecific, familiar vs unfamiliar, individual vs group member. mori's "medium peak" is really interaction with heterospecifics that share many human attributes (e.g. domesticated animals); the "maximum peak" is conspecifics . conspecifics are judged far more selectively, which is why the maximum peak has a narrower base. 3. the paradox : passing the valley does not solve anything, because technology will keep going. robots that reach and exceed human performance fall into a second uncanny valley on the far side. the landscape is symmetric. convergence on humanness should be replaced by divergence. 4. the escape : go around the peak. determine the robot's function and environment first and design the best-suited agent regardless of human similarity — function-orientedness. ethologically, the robot occupies its own niche . 5. dogs demonstrate this works. domestication (~18,800–32,100 years) produced an agent that is morphologically and behaviourally very different from humans yet has enough social-competence to integrate into human society. breeds occupy specific behavioural niches. both species retained independent capacity to evolve; competition is limited (dog-human-interaction-model). key definitions - social competence — "an individual's ability to generate social skills that conform to the expectations of others and the social rules of the group." emerges only if the individual wants to participate, has the means, and is regarded by others as able to participate. - partnership is a process, not a state. "a social robot does not automatically become a social partner but achieves this state of affairs if it engages in the appropriate kind of social interactions." not an a priori attribute of the robot (interspecific-hri). dog-derived skills proposed for robots: attachment to humans, simple communicative interaction, responsiveness to learning and training, and being useful in some specific way. why the alternatives fail the paper rejects the "expose infants to robots early" route explicitly — it is unrealistic, unethical, and risks confusing the human social recognition system, potentially producing misguided social and sexual preferences later in life. limitations - a theoretical paper. it proposes a research programme and…
panksepp-2005-affective-consciousness: jaak panksepp, affective consciousness: core emotional feelings in animals and humans , consciousness and cognition 14(1):30–80 , march 2005. doi:10.1016/j.concog.2004.10.004 reference [8] of research-proposal, now held. the wiki carried panksepp second-hand via szabo-2011-emotional-engine for a week; this is the primary, and it is the fuller theoretical statement. its companion, panksepp-2011-emotional-circuits, is the shorter and later summary. takeaways - the seven systems, first-hand : seeking, fear, rage, lust, care, panic, play. confirms the list the wiki had via szabó. described as "the neurodynamic attractor landscapes of a variety of extended trans-diencephalic, limbic emotional action systems". - a terminological hierarchy the wiki has been missing. emotion is the umbrella term covering "affective, cognitive, behavioral, expressive, and a host of physiological changes". affect is "the subjective experiential-feeling component". and affects divide into emotional (linked to internal brain action states, triggered by environmental events), homeostatic (bodily — hunger, thirst) and sensory (taste, touch). see q2 below. - three psychological dimensions are acknowledged : valence, arousal, and "surgency or power (how much does a certain feeling fill one's mental life)" . panksepp is not a purely discrete theorist — he names a dimensional description and then argues the causal structure is circuit-based. - "there is currently no agreed upon taxonomy of affective states." worth quoting when the thesis has to justify picking one. - six defining characteristics of an emotional system (fig. 1): unconditional sensory access; instinctual motor outputs; modulation of sensory inputs (incentive salience); positive feedback components that sustain arousal after the precipitating event has passed ; modulation by cognitive inputs; and the capacity to modify and channel cognitive activity. - primary / secondary / tertiary consciousness. primary = raw sensory/perceptual feelings and internal emotional experience; secondary = thoughts about experiences; tertiary = thoughts about thoughts, largely human and language-dependent. - dual-aspect monism (spinozan): emotional feelings reflect the neurodynamics of the brain systems that generate instinctual emotional behaviour. this is the methodological premise that licenses reading affect off behaviour — the same move ethorobotics makes when it reads emotion off robot movement. - the capitalisation convention is argued, not stylistic : capitals designate specific neural systems , and guard against "part–whole confusions" — the error of assuming a circuit explains everything the vernacular word connotes. the rpe contradiction, now doubly and directly sourced §7 of this paper is titled: the seeking/expectancy/wanting system of the brain: it's not just "reward prediction error" and the body states that emotional systems are "unlikely that they can be encapsulated by the concept of reinforcement or even more subtle…
panksepp-2011-emotional-circuits: jaak panksepp, the basic emotional circuits of mammalian brains: do animals have affective lives? , neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews 35(9):1791–1804 , 2011. doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2011.08.003 a festschrift essay for a special issue celebrating panksepp's cross-species affective neuroscience at bowling green state university. shorter and later than panksepp-2005-affective-consciousness; read both, cite the 2005 paper for theory and this one for the per-circuit descriptions. not on the research-proposal reference list — csenge supplied it alongside the 2005 paper. takeaways - thumbnail descriptions of all seven circuits , the most usable per-system summary in the corpus. see panksepp-affective-systems for the table. - a three-level hierarchy : primary-process (evolutionary "tools for living"), secondary-process (unconscious learning and memory), tertiary-process (higher cognition). mixing levels is his central methodological complaint. - seven defining attributes of an emotional system (fig. 4), including that "emotions outlast the stimuli that activated the systems" — which is exactly the temporal-dynamics layer szabo-2011-emotional-engine built by hand with peak widths and decline rates, and it now has a source. - the "law of affect" : "'rewards' and 'punishments' would not work unless they changed the way animals feel affectively." affect is proposed as the mechanism of reinforcement, not a by-product of it. bears directly on q15 in open-questions — it is an argument for the emotional engine being the reward function rather than a state feature. - play builds social competence : "a key function of the social play system is to help young animals to acquire the social knowledge and refinement of subtle social interactions that they will need to thrive... may be one of the major emotional forces that promotes the epigenetic construction of higher social brain functions." see social-competence. - seeking wants to learn but wants nothing in particular : "this system does not 'want' anything specific before learning; it just wants opportunities to explore the world... it should be emphasized that this system 'wants' to learn, is designed to learn automatically." - decortication leaves emotional-instinctual urges intact while severely impairing instrumental learning; "many forms of classical conditioning survive". that maps onto the prediction/control split in conditioning. - repeats the rpe objection recorded on panksepp-2005-affective-consciousness. two corrections this forces on the wiki [!warning] nobody has mapped the inter-circuit interactions "all primal emotional systems interact with each other in primal inhibitory and excitatory relationships that no one has yet mapped empirically ." panksepp-affective-systems previously claimed that "inter-circuit inhibition gives a principled basis for arbitration rules". it does not — there is no map to base rules on. corrected on that page; plutchik-1982-psychoevolutionary: robert plutchik, a psychoevolutionary theory of emotions , social science information 21(4–5):529–553 , 1982. doi:10.1177/053901882021004003 reference [9] of research-proposal, now held. a summary of plutchik's 1980 book emotion: a psychoevolutionary synthesis , prepared for a conference on "the nature and function of emotion" convened by klaus scherer and paul ekman (bad homburg, 6–10 july 1981). [!warning] this paper has no chaseable citations it states outright that it is a summary and that "for references to other work cited in the paper the reader is referred to plutchik (1980)". the reference list contains only plutchik's own works. every empirical result reported here — block's semantic-differential study, conte's paired comparisons, the chimpanzee epi work — is second-hand and untraceable from this document. cite the theory from here; do not cite the evidence from here without obtaining plutchik (1980). logged in citation-backlog. takeaways - emotion is a hypothetical construct, not a feeling report. five arguments against defining emotion by verbal report: reports may deceive; repression creates false negatives; reports depend on conditioning history and verbal facility; emotions are attributed to infants, animals and the mentally ill who cannot report; and "emotions are rarely if ever experienced in a pure state" . - three languages for describing the same emotional state — subjective, behavioural, and functional . this is the most useful single contribution to this thesis; research-proposal: first-party source. states the thesis, the theoretical commitments, and the claimed novelty. everything currently in this wiki traces back here, which means the wiki is currently unvalidated against published literature — that is the first gap to close. takeaways - positions the work inside ethorobotics : technology built on ethological findings, treating hri as an interspecific interaction and committing to function-orientedness over human imitation. - dogs as the model species for robot social behaviour, justified by their understanding of ostensive-signalling and their reading of human vocal and visual emotional expression. - emotion attribution to artificial agents facilitates interaction — the premise licensing an affective layer at all (emotion-attribution). - the system must fuse two input streams : perceived human affect, and the robot's own internal state (battery, sensor and motor health). fusing proprioceptive-style signals with social perception is the distinctive move here — most affective hri work models only the human. - two candidate grounding models named: panksepp-affective-systems and plutchik-model. the choice is left open — this is the live decision. - implementation lineage: fuzzy-logic emotion engines, extensible with transfer learning; behaviour-trees for emotion-based decision-making. - validation is on human subjects (validation-study). claimed novelty real-time event detection in real environments , as against lab-bound implementations. this is the claim the wiki should be hardest on: every ingested system needs assessing for where it was validated and at what latency. limitations of this source - unpublished, unreviewed, and self-authored — it establishes intent, not fact. - references [1] – [10] are cited by number with no bibliography supplied . all ten are unresolved;
